name: git clean
shortDescription: Remove untracked files from the working tree. Helps keep your working directory pristine.
detailedDescription:
While `git reset --hard` clears away changes to tracked files, it leaves untracked files alone. If you want a completely pristine working directory (like a fresh clone), you need `git clean`.

This command recursively removes files that are not under version control. Because this permanently deletes files from your disk (not moving them to the trash), it is inherently dangerous. Git requires the `-f` (force) flag to actually delete anything, unless your configuration explicitly allows it.

Always run with `-n` (dry-run) first to see what will be deleted.

parameters.description: Don't actually remove anything, just show what WOULD be done. ALWAYS run this first.
Actually execute the deletion. Required by default.
Also remove untracked directories, not just files.
Remove ALL untracked files, including those ignored by .gitignore (like build artifacts or node_modules).
Remove ONLY files ignored by .gitignore. Useful for cleaning build products without touching new source files.

examples.title: Safe cleanup workflow
examples.description: Always check what will be deleted before forcing.
examples.code:
# 1. See what will be deleted
git clean -n -d

# 2. If it looks correct, delete them
git clean -f -d

examples.title: The ultimate reset (Pristine state)
examples.description: Revert the repo to exactly how it looks on the remote.
examples.code:
# Revert all tracked files:
git reset --hard HEAD

# Delete all untracked AND ignored files:
git clean -f -d -x

# Your repo is now a perfectly clean slate

commonMistakes.text: Files deleted with `git clean` are NOT stored in Git history or your OS trash bin. They are permanently gone. Always use `-n` first.
